extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers interested in philosophy, ethics, and Montaigne's essays
extracted.subtask_description: A reflective Renaissance essay (Montaigne) exploring the nature and qualities of perfect friendship versus ordinary acquaintance, and a separate chapter on the ethical requirement for moderation in virtue and pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary versus imposed friendships
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendships imposed by law or natural obligation (e.g., father/son, brothers) lack the voluntary choice that produces true affection; voluntary liberty most promptly produces affection and friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast familial or legally-mandated ties with voluntarily chosen friendships: the former have less of our own choice and voluntary freedom. (Original phrasing: "those are friendships that the law and natural obligation impose upon us, so much less is there of our own choice and voluntary freedom; whereas that voluntary liberty of ours has no production more promptly and, properly its own than affection and friendship.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship as temperate, equal, and constant
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship is 'a general and universal fire, but temperate and equal, a constant established heat, all gentle and smooth, without poignancy or roughness,' in contrast to romantic love which is more active, precipitant, fickle and inconstant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate affections by their stability and moderation: friend-like affection should be even, temperate, and enduring rather than feverish or subject to paroxysms (comparison to romantic love is used as negative example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fruition destroys romantic desire; friendship grows with enjoyment
rubrics_metrics.description: Romantic desire is often 'frantic' and directed at what flees from us; once fruition occurs it vanishes (subject to satiety). Friendship, being spiritual, is nourished and improved by enjoyment and increases with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a criterion, prefer bonds that are sustained and strengthened by shared enjoyment rather than those that are exhausted by possession or consummation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect friendship is indivisible and exclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect friendship 'possesses the whole soul' and cannot admit of a rival; it is indivisible — one cannot love two different persons with that same exclusive, whole-soul devotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exclusivity as a mark of the deepest friendship: attempts to 'multiply' a unique friendship into several equal ones are unrealistic and contrary to the nature of that singular bond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute concurrence of wills and commonality of goods
rubrics_metrics.description: In perfect friendship 'all things, wills, thoughts, opinions, goods, wives, children, honours, and lives' become effectively common between friends; the union deprives them of the concept of benefits, obligations, thanks or exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the depth of friendship by the degree to which friends act with a single will and eschew transactional relationships; examples include wills giving friends the opportunity to confer benefits (Eudamidas) and Diogenes' remark about redemanding money of friends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete mutual knowledge and trust
rubrics_metrics.description: True friends know one another's intentions and dispositions so well that 'no one action of his... could not presently, and at first sight, find out the moving cause.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess friendship quality by mutual insight and anticipatory understanding of the other's motives (Laelius/Blosius example shows the depth of trust). This knowledge grounds willingness to 'obey' or act for a friend in hypothetical extreme cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ordinary friendships and apply prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary, customary friendships require caution: 'you are to walk with bridle in your hand, with prudence and circumspection'—they are not the same as the sovereign/perfect friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply different standards to ordinary acquaintances (expect transactional supports, present-giving, reciprocal favors) versus the rare, sovereign friendship; follow Chilo's pragmatic advice to be prepared for changes in ordinary friendships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendships should be fortified by judgement and time
rubrics_metrics.description: Only those friendships 'that are fortified and confirmed by judgement and the length of time' deserve to be reputed true friendships (Cicero quoted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use duration and the exercise of sound judgement about the friend's character as evidentiary grounds when recognizing a friendship as genuine and durable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose associates by relevance to the role
rubrics_metrics.description: When confederations hold by a single end, select persons based on qualities relevant to that end (e.g., when hiring a footman care about diligence, not chastity; physician's religion is irrelevant to his professional role).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pragmatically evaluate people for specific functions by the competencies that matter to the task rather than irrelevant personal attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual preferences in companionship
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferences for companions vary by context: for table-talk prefer the witty to the grave learned; in bed prefer beauty before goodness; in common discourse prefer the ablest speaker regardless of sincerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select companions and value traits according to situational utility and pleasure; Montaigne candidly admits differing priorities in different social situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation: excess in virtue becomes vice
rubrics_metrics.description: One may be excessive even in virtue; 'there is never any excess in virtue' is a verbal trick—if virtue is pursued beyond proper bounds it becomes harmful or vicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge actions by a balance criterion: both deficiency and excess are faults; examples include parents/commanders who enact extreme punishments in the name of virtue (Pausanias' mother, Posthumius) as cautionary cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit philosophical zeal to profitable bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Callicles' warning: the extremity of philosophy is hurtful—taken beyond limits of profit it can render one brutish, contemptuous of laws and human pleasures, unfit for public administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the practice of philosophy and abstract sciences by their practical consequences; prefer a moderate engagement that is useful and pleasant rather than destructive to social functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugal pleasures should be sober and conscientious
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriage is a solemn and religious tie; the pleasure from it should be 'a sober and serious delight, and mixed with a certain kind of gravity'—immoderate, indecent or debauched sexual practices are reproachable even within marriage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate marital conduct by sobriety and discretion; admonishes against licentious tricks and heedless excess even in lawful relations (advises plain, conscientious behavior).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/legal restraints may recommend sexual moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some theological and cultural rules curb conjugal indulgence (e.g., condemnations of intercourse within certain forbidden degrees, or customs forbidding intercourse with pregnant women or during menses); such restraints are sometimes justified to prevent immoderate affection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that diverse customs and religious injunctions serve as external means to enforce moderation in sexuality and avoid excesses that could otherwise pass into imprudence.
